title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- a representative regional centenary address CJP delivered as overall chair at the Baguio City Convention Center on April 4, 2001 to some 3,000 personnel of Judicial Regions 1 and 2, urging celebration coupled with a pledge to implement judicial reforms

The founding-date rationale: June 11, 1901 (Act 136, the Judiciary Law, enacted by the civil-government Second Philippine Commission) is chosen over the earlier May 29, 1899 General Order No. 20 of military governor Gen. Elwell Otis, because Act 136 established an independent judicial hierarchy and 'we treasure independence as a basic feature of our judicial system'

The case-delay problem and backlog statistics: while the SC cut its own backlog from ~2,000 (1996) to ~300, the lower courts fared worse (Court of Appeals, second-level and first-level courts all showed large net case pile-ups for 1995-1999); causes include one-third of trial courts being vacant and the flood of Batas Pambansa 22 bouncing-check cases

The reform agenda and an anti-complacency exhortation: computers for trial courts, national professors of law, Halls of Justice, exemption from the Salary Standardization Law, an improved disciplinary process and ADR -- closing with Bishop Benny Tudtud's prayer 'Disturb Us O Lord' and the maxim that 'the reward for good work is more work'
sub_topics: The Baguio regional celebration (Regions 1 and 2): ~3,000 court officials and employees gathered; CJP's appeal to celebrate not with mere 'temporary merriment' but with a pledge to implement reforms

Founding-date rationale: Act 136 (June 11, 1901) vested judicial power in the SC, Courts of First Instance and Justice of the Peace Courts; chosen over Gen. Elwell Otis's General Order No. 20 (May 29, 1899), which was 'really nothing more than an extension of the military authority of the United States Army'

Trial courts as 'the backbone of the judicial branch': CJP likens trial judges, clerks, sheriffs and process servers to 'the marines and the foot soldiers in the front line,' who face 'weary litigants, their sometimes arrogant lawyers, the critical media and the expectant general public'

Speedy dispensation of quality justice as the most visible reform; delay as a longstanding worldwide complaint (citing an International Herald Tribune report of an Asian country needing 324 years to clear its dockets)

Backlog defined (cases submitted more than 24 months -- the SC's constitutional deadline; 3 months for trial courts); the SC's own reduction from ~2,000 to ~300, hoped to be eliminated by June 11, 2001

Transparency about the lower courts: Court of Appeals net pile-up of 3,088 (1995-1999); second-level courts (RTC, CTA, Shari'ah District) ~35,000 net increase; first-level courts ~324,174 over five years

Causes of the pile-up: one-third of trial courts vacant for lack of qualified applicants (low salaries and poor peace-and-order); the swamping of first-level courts with Batas Pambansa 22 bouncing-check cases, prompting an SC circular discouraging use of courts 'as a collection agency for rubber checks'

Reform measures listed: SC-authorized computers for all RTCs (with software accessing all SC decisions from 1901), national professors of law, continuing education, Halls of Justice, raising salaries by exempting the judiciary from the Salary Standardization Law, an improved disciplinary process, and ADR

The appeal to the frontline: judges should attend to their own backlogs, hold hearings diligently, encourage amicable settlement and decide within the reglementary period -- 'if the Supreme Court can eliminate its own backlog, the lower courts will be able to follow suit'

Pride tempered by anti-complacency: the impeachment trial made legal phrases part of lay vocabulary and made Davide 'the most credible Filipino'; yet CJP closes with Bishop Benny Tudtud's prayer 'Disturb Us O Lord' to warn against resting on laurels -- 'the reward for good work is more work'

stances.claim: The judiciary dates its founding to June 11, 1901 (Act 136) rather than to Gen. Otis's May 29, 1899 General Order No. 20, because the latter was 'really nothing more than an extension of the military authority of the United States Army' while Act 136 was enacted by a civil government and established an independent judicial hierarchy; 'since we treasure independence as a basic feature of our judicial system, we have chosen June 11, 1901.'
stances.rhetorical_move: independence-as-the-founding-criterion, now sharpened by an explicit rejected alternative (the Otis military order) to dramatize that independence, not mere prior existence, defines the institution's birth
stances.confidence: asserted as the Court's settled institutional self-understanding

stances.claim: A centenary must not be 'temporary merriment'; pride in 100 years of competence and integrity is warranted, but 'we cannot rest on these laurels' -- reform and the elevation of standards are 'never complete,' and 'the reward for good work is more work.' Complacency is the enemy of an institution that has just earned the public's highest approval.
stances.rhetorical_move: anti-complacency exhortation, secured by Bishop Tudtud's 'Disturb Us O Lord' prayer as a spiritual warrant against self-satisfaction
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing moral of the regional celebrations

stances.claim: The court system should not be misused 'as a collection agency for rubber checks'; the banking sector should solve unpaid-check problems by other means, such as banning habitual bad-check writers from maintaining checking accounts (as in the US), rather than swamping first-level courts with Batas Pambansa 22 cases.
stances.rhetorical_move: docket-protection argument: reframing a criminal-law caseload as a misallocation of judicial resources better solved by banking-sector self-regulation
stances.confidence: asserted as the rationale behind an SC sentencing circular

notable_anecdotes: The rejected founding date: a year before Act 136, US military governor Gen. Elwell Otis issued General Order No. 20 (May 29, 1899) creating a 'Supreme Court' and naming its members -- but the judiciary declined to date itself from that order because it was merely an extension of US Army authority, choosing instead the independent, civil-government Act 136.

The 324-year docket: CJP cites an International Herald Tribune report that in one Asian country about 25 million cases were pending, so that 'even if no new actions were filed, 324 years would be needed to clear the dockets' -- a foil that makes the Philippine backlog look comparatively manageable.

The lower-court candor: in a 'measure of transparency,' CJP discloses unflattering numbers -- a Court of Appeals net pile-up of 3,088 and a first-level-court increase of roughly 324,174 cases over 1995-1999 -- even amid a celebration, refusing to let the festivities obscure the problem.

Bouncing checks and vacant courts: he notes that first-level courts are 'swamped' with Batas Pambansa 22 cases and that one-third of all trial courts sit vacant because low salaries and poor peace-and-order conditions deter qualified lawyers.

The 'Disturb Us O Lord' close: CJP recites a favorite prayer he attributes to the late Bishop Benny Tudtud -- a plea to be disturbed 'when our dreams have come true because we dreamed too little' -- to remind a proud audience that 'the reward for good work is more work.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces a representative regional centenary address CJP delivered as overall chair at the Baguio City Convention Center on April 4, 2001 before some 3,000 personnel of Judicial Regions 1 and 2. He opens by explaining the founding-date rationale: the judiciary reckons its birth to June 11, 1901 (Act 136, the Judiciary Law, enacted by the civil-government Second Philippine Commission) rather than to Gen. Elwell Otis's earlier General Order No. 20 of May 29, 1899, which was 'really nothing more than an extension of the military authority of the United States Army' -- 'since we treasure independence as a basic feature of our judicial system, we have chosen June 11, 1901.' Calling trial courts 'the backbone of the judicial branch' and likening their personnel to 'the marines and the foot soldiers in the front line,' he urges that the centenary be more than 'temporary merriment' and presses the most visible reform -- the speedy dispensation of quality justice. With candor 'as a measure of transparency,' he reports that while the SC cut its own backlog from ~2,000 to ~300, the lower courts pile up cases (a Court of Appeals net of 3,088 and roughly 324,174 first-level cases over 1995-1999), blaming one-third of trial courts sitting vacant for low pay and poor peace-and-order, and the flood of Batas Pambansa 22 bouncing-check cases -- the court system, he insists, should not be 'a collection agency for rubber checks.' He surveys the reform agenda (computers for all RTCs accessing SC decisions back to 1901, national professors of law, Halls of Justice, exemption from the Salary Standardization Law, an improved disciplinary process and ADR) and appeals to judges to clear their own backlogs. Proud that the impeachment trial made Davide 'the most credible Filipino' and the SC the highest-rated institution, he nonetheless warns against resting on laurels, closing with Bishop Benny Tudtud's prayer 'Disturb Us O Lord' and the maxim that 'the reward for good work is more work.'
